newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seen aiding new North Korea food appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen aiding new North Korea food appeal.

text.p: The World Food Programme has formally appealed for $41.6 million in new food aid for North Korea and the United States was certain to make a contribution, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

"I understand the World Food Programme today issued a new emergency appeal for humanitarian assistance to North Korea. The World Food Programme is seeking donations of 100,000 metric tons of food valued at roughly $41.6 million," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Burns, noting that Washington responded positively to all other previous food appeals for North Korea, said the administration was "seriously" studying the request and would make a decision very soon. A senior official, speaking anonymously, added: "I believe the United States will make a decision to contribute."

Burns said Washington believed there was a food crisis in North Korea. He said the new appeal was designed to feed 1.7 million North Korean civilians, including 630,000 children under the age of five.

He acknowledged that the World Food Programme, a U.N. agency, had limited its appeal to only a fraction of North Korea's needs, estimated at 2.3 million tons. This was because "they want to focus on meeting the immediate needs of targeted groups and they have targeted young children," he said.
Experts say the small size of the appeal compared to the need reflected the difficulty of persuading key donors like the United States and South Korea to give anything at all.

Burns said it would be impossible for the World Food Programme to meet all of the Stalinist state's acute food needs, brought to a crisis by massive floods in 1995 and 1996. As a result, donations, such as those collected by the World Food Programme, must be supplemented by commercial purchases by Pyongyang, he said.
A South Korean spokesman said on Monday his government would also consider sending food aid to famine-striken North Korea if the World Food Programme made a formal appeal.

"We have not decided what the item will be, how much it will be, or when and how the aid will be sent," the South Korean spokesman said. "But we will positively consider sending aid if an appeal is made by international organisations."

Burns said it was not known how large the U.S. donation might be. But sources have said Washington was expected to donate at least $8.425 million; South Korea, about $3 million, and Japan, about $6 million -- roughly the same as last year.

North Korea has been negotiating with the Minnneapolis-based grain exporter, Cargill Inc. to acquire 500,000 tons of grain in a barter deal but that deal is now stalled, making Pyongyang even more eager to receive donations from the international community.

North Korea's ambassador to the United Nations, in an interview with CNN last week, charged that a briefing on the U.S.-South Korean proposal for Korean Peninsula peace talks was twice delayed because Washington had not carried through on its promise to provide food aid.

The United States insisted it never promised Pyongyang a specific amount of food aid in return for North Korea's participation in the briefing, which was aimed at bringing North and South into a dialogue to forge permanent peace on the peninsula, divided in the 1950-53 Korean War.

But after North Korea apologised for a September submarine infiltration into South Korea, Washington gave Cargill Inc. permission to barter 500,000 tons of grain with North Korea. Those negotiations have bogged down over financing for the deal and the adminstration has refused to become involved in what it has called "commercial transactions" between North Korea and Cargill.
Burns insisted a formal decision on the World Food Program's latest food aid appeal for North Korea would be based solely on humanitarian considerations.
